title: After a massive 2021 office expansion, Bungie is now trying to sublease its 211,000 square foot headquarters
summary: Bungie says it "will continue to maintain a physical office presence in Bellevue."
body: In 2021, as studio CEO Pete Parsons cited the company's recent "tremendous growth and opportunity," Bungie announced its plans for a massive expansion to its Bellevue, Washington headquarters . The campus embiggening, which internal sources have reportedly described as costing "hundreds of millions" of dollars, more than doubled the size of Bungie's offices from 84,000 square feet to just under 211,000. Now, after five and a half years of spending sprees, publisher acquisitions, stumbling product launches, project cancellations, and repeated mass layoffs, Bungie appears to be seeking subletters for the goliath game development headquarters it's no longer capable of filling. According to a 10-page leasing brochure reviewed by The Game Post , Bungie is seeking interested renters to sublease its expansive headquarters, listing its 210,984 square feet as a "turn-key" production facility. In addition to expected office fixtures, the listing also features a dedicated lobby, gym and exercise facilities (including a rock climbing wall), a motion-capture studio, a cafe, catering space, and a private exterior patio. While the brochure didn't directly identify the studio, a statement provide…

title: A popular streamer turned down a 6-figure deal to play Arc Raiders because 'the game frustrated me so much'
summary: Seven-figures? Now we're talking.
body: Everyone has a price. Maybe it's $100, maybe it's $1,000, maybe it's for someone to see your innate value as a human being, or maybe it's $1,000,000. Popular streamer TimTheTatman recently revealed what it would take to get him to go back to Arc Raiders , and spoilers, it's not the third option. There was apparently an ad deal floating around for the Arc Raiders and Subway collab, which TimTheTatman was approached for, but did not entertain. "I did say no to six-figures with Arc Raiders, I did," he revealed in a stream earlier this week. "I said 'No thank you'. And it was the Subway Arc Raiders ad. I said I just can't do it, I'm sorry." (Image credit: Embark) This was met with the exact response you'd expect with people being baffled that he'd ever think of turning down such a lucrative offer. "That's kind of the funny part of being in a streamer position," TimTheTatman continued. "People say 'you're a fucking sellout' but then in the same breath I said I passed on six-figures from Arc Raiders and people are like 'you're fucking stupid'." title: Great, now motherboard prices might be next to spike thanks to component costs increasing by up to 50%
summary: PC gaming sure ain't cheap.
body: PC gaming has always been an expensive hobby, but prices have become downright ridiculous as of late. It's bad enough that Nvidia's RTX 50-series cards cost slightly less than an international flight , but the memory supply crisis is also driving up the price of RAM and SSDs . Now it looks like motherboards might be next to see a significant price spike. Board Channels is a forum for hardware manufacturers and partners to communicate. One poster recently wrote , "The price of upstream raw materials for motherboards has indeed risen significantly." They go on to say that the price of motherboard PCBs alone has increased by between 15% and 50% . Wi-Fi modules are said to have gone up between 10% and 20%, while capacitor prices have also gone up approximately 50% (via Videocardz ). As we've reported before, these price increases are likely caused by material shortages resulting from the Strait of Hormuz crisis and the ongoing Iran war . For instance, PPE resin can be thought of as the glue that binds the many layers of a PCB together, and a huge chunk of the world's high-quality PPE comes from petrochemical company Saudi Basic Industries Corporation (SABIC) in Saudi Arabia. body: Last week, in the wake of a rash of developer hardware thefts at this year's Gamescom, the event's organizers provoked a wave of outcry by publishing a statement that many perceived as callously placing the blame on exhibitors who hadn't adequately insured their equipment. Today, Gamescom released an additional statement on X, admitting that its initial response was inadequate and committing to improving the rigor of its security procedures with input from affected exhibitors. pic.twitter.com/lOxBnmMplB September 4, 2026 "Over the past few days, we have received a great deal of criticism for the way we communicated about the theft of hardware belonging to several indie developers. That criticism is justified," Gamescom said. "Our first response did not strike the right tone, and it did not show the people affected the empathy they deserved. We are sorry." title: In a sea of failed live service games, I'm shocked to see someone trying to make a MOBA
summary: Project Zeta is trying to crack a near-impenetrable market.
body: Making a live service game these days feels like trying to shoot an arrow at a flea while blindfolded. Striking gold with a hot new shooter or other team-based multiplayer game with a quirky twist seems like an exercise in futility, but that isn't stopping developers and publishers from trying to be the next big thing. Personally, if I was trying to enter an already-volatile market, I'd probably be steering well clear of MOBAs. They're finicky, have a high barrier to entry, and require a ridiculous amount of time commitment to ever be remotely good at them. Even then, dragging a League or Dota player away from their game to try another one is a big ask. Hell, I'm still shocked Deadlock has managed to do it. (Image credit: Krafton) So I don't know whether to applaud developer Nirvanana for giving it a go with Project Zeta, or grab the team by the shoulders and give them a good old shake for doing something I perceive to be utterly reckless. Though, as Nirvanana will maintain, Project Zeta isn't quite a MOBA. As the developer tells me, it's actually a 4v4 multi-team tactical arena battle. Not battle royale, just battle. "We tried not to be tied down to those traditional things," Nir…

title: Age Twisters is a simple yet charming spin on the co-op adventure that aims to feel like watching a Pixar movie
summary: The puzzles won't stump you, but Piccolo Studios says they're not supposed to.
body: As I'm making my way through the beginning of two-player co-op adventure Age Twisters alongside the founders of developer Piccolo Studios, I'm told the goal was to create a game that evokes the same feelings as watching a Pixar movie with your child. Now I am admittedly sprogless, but it wasn't difficult to latch onto those similar fuzzy feelings of nostalgia and familial love even as I completed puzzles alongside a man I'd only met minutes prior. Age Twisters is the studio's attempt at a game like It Takes Two or Split Fiction, albeit much lower on the toughness scale—something which the developer itself admits, instead going for a game that's constantly evolving and different rather than outright difficult. It takes a granddaughter-grandfather duo and slaps a couple of age-bending bracelets on them, allowing each one to age up or down all the way from a young child to a hobbling old bean. (Image credit: Krafton) It's a wonderfully novel mechanic—each age has its own portrait, voice acting, and dynamic dialogue that'll shift as you age up or down across the story. Each even comes with their own quirks. I attempted to jump over a gap as an old lady but was unable to, and similarly…

title: Arc Raiders' executive producer admits its developers 'couldn't keep pace with the players' and their need for content, but promises Frozen Trail as the answer
summary: "What we want to do is spend more time building quality stuff."
body: If there's one thing you should never underestimate, it's a gamer's love for completing little tasks. Whether it's battle passes, meaningless fetch quests, or in Arc Raiders' case, its expeditions. There's just the right amount of dopamine involved for a neuron activation, so you best bet that they'll rip through them at an unthinkable speed. I'll concede that Embark Studios probably couldn't have foreseen the full extent of this love prior to Arc Raiders release, but still, the outcome is the same: gamers out-growing their once-beloved game because they managed to complete all their tasks way too fast. (Image credit: Embark) "We didn’t really expect that amount of players to show up and play ARC Raiders," executive producer Aleksander Grøndal explains in an interview with GamesBeat . "That surprised us. We were a bit unprepared. That’s one of the hard lessons we had to learn. When January came and some of the problems started with the game." January saw the first crack in Arc Raiders' armour, as the novelty began to wear off and players became more keenly aware of how limited its content was alongside growing concerns about cheating and stream sniping . title: Nvidia puts its money where its mouth is on open weight AI, moving to buy Hugging Face for $13 billion
summary: Come on guys, fling a few mil my way?
body: Nvidia has just announced that it intends to acquire Hugging Face, the biggest open platform dedicated to developing machine-learning applications. Considering Nvidia has been all-in on AI for the past few years—to the point that I barely remember the last time the company even mentioned gaming in an earnings call—it's hardly a surprising move. What did encourage a sharp intake of breath from me though was the price of this purchase; Nvidia will buy Hugging Face for a total of $12,930,300,000 . $11.9 billion of that will go to Hugging Face's investors, while employees that join Nvidia will be offered an ‌equity-based retention ⁠program of up to $1 billion, according to Reuters . But even though there's billions of dollars in the mix, that doesn't mean the walls are about to come down around Hugging Face. "Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang writes, "Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want. title: Stalker 2 studio is raffling keychains made from a shot-down Russian helicopter to raise funds for mine removal in the real-world Chornobyl Exclusion Zone
summary: Other prizes include patches, t-shirts, and game keys—GSC Game World hopes to raise at least $100,000 for the effort.
body: Stalker 2 studio GSC Game World has joined with Ukrainian charity United24 on a new fundraising initiative that aims to raise $100,000 to help fund efforts to remove mines and other explosive devices from the real-world Chornobyl Exclusion Zone. The Zone—the real one—was established in 1986 following the disaster at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant. It's not quite as fanciful as the videogame counterpart but it is hazardous, and public access is restricted; as one of the most radioactively contaminated regions on the planet, it's also of considerable scientific interest. Facilities in the zone also require ongoing maintenance, which became a problem when Russian troops seized the Zone and power plant during the early days of the invasion of Ukraine. The troops withdrew a couple months later—some reportedly received "significant doses" of radiation during their time there—leaving behind mines and explosives that pose a significant hazard to returning workers and researchers: United24 says at least eight explosions have wounded or killed staff and soldiers since the Russian withdrawal. title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation gets a release date and a proper look at its airship overworld, which is cool, if in danger of inducing open world fatigue
summary: The Remake trilogy's a long one.
body: If there's one thing that's become daunting about the modern RPG, it's the ballooning time investment. There's no better example than the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy, a reimagining of a classic that has stretched itself out between three entire fully-fledged games. Final Fantasy 7 Revelation just had its release date dropped alongside a 10-minute gameplay deep dive during PlayStation's State of Play . In it, we got to see a closer look at the airship overworld. It's pretty dang impressive. Your airship'll let you zip around the open world in record time, showing you a charming mini-model of each zone—it's not one hundred percent seamless (there's a cutscene between choosing a landing spot and parachuting down that's doubtless there to disguise some loading) but the ability to parachute down anywhere is neat, and it feels like a modern-day realisation of what the classic airship overworld of older RPGs were trying to do. We saw this in practice in a couple of locations, including Wutai—wherein Yuffie was able to grapple hook to a nearby roof and have a roam around. And yet, despite how impressive this all looks, I can't help but feel a certain dread set in. I haven't played FF7 …

title: Alien: Isolation 2's Gamescom demo kept its cards close to its chest, but I'm definitely ready to be terrified again
summary: Just, you know, give me a minute to collect myself.
body: It's like seeing an old friend: the clanking in the vents over your head, the way the ribbed tail passes over objects with a thunk-ka-thunk-ka-thunk-ka-thunk , the head-within-a-head, the screaming. You are here, you are back, you have been impaled through the abdomen and killed. I have played perhaps 20 minutes of Alien: Isolation 2 at Gamescom 2026 and I can tell you this: it is certainly Alien: Isolation. There are some new wrinkles, though—where the first game was a strictly inside affair, stranding you on the space station Sevastopol, the second game sets you down planetside in an entirely new character's shoes. Fewer air vents, fewer vital systems shuddering to a halt; a lot more weather, a lot more space. You are Blake. Here are the two things to know about Blake: she is not Amanda Ripley—the first game's protagonist who did not feature at all in my time with Alien: Isolation 2—but she is Weyland-Yutani. Specifically, she's Weyland-Yutani management, and isn't that interesting? You're no working class hero. You're now in the shoes of a character who, in any Alien movie worth its salt, would likely reveal themselves as a villain and end up decapitated about 70% of the way th…

title: Onimusha on Steam Deck is the definition of 'playable': Surprisingly pleasant, so long as 30 fps isn't a dealbreaker
summary: Capcom flaunts the flexibility of the RE Engine again.
body: We're long past the days of assuming the Steam Deck can comfortably handle the new big-budget action game of the moment, but here's a nice surprise: Valve's handheld is not a bad way to play Onimusha: Way of the Sword. It's not quite the optimization darling that Resident Evil Requiem was earlier this year, but it's much better news than Monster Hunter Wilds or Dragon's Dogma 2. After testing Onimusha in its taxing Kyoto hub area, I'd add this to the win column for Capcom's proprietary engine. To set expectations: Onimusha is a stubbornly 30-40 fps game on Deck. It can get as high as the 50s and 60s in the right conditions—turning FSR 3.1.4 upscaling on while in corridor areas outside the main hub—but you will eventually shoot back down to the 30s when there's a lot of action on screen. So if you're of the mind that a lower, stable framerate is ultimately the most comfortable way to play a game, then you can confidently lock it at 30 fps and turn off the performance overlay. That's how I played a decent chunk of it over the last few days, pausing here and there to see which graphical bumps I could get away with. The default configuration cranks everything down to its lowest settin…

title: CD Projekt Red isn't 'planning to rely on AI making complete games', and will still be 'predominantly using people' for The Witcher 4 and beyond
summary: "I think everybody has to make those judgments on their own."
body: Generative AI in videogame development, despite the looming potentiality of a bubble popping , has continued to be a hot-button topic pelted at developers during earning calls, despite most of them recognising that there's not much use for it beyond mundane busywork. Sure, it's being used commonly , but rarely for the actual making of the videogame itself. Filling in the roles that procedural generation might or, like, resizing shoulderpads—or for "user preference analysis" . Not exactly the kind of stuff that revolutionises an industry, and certainly not enough to justify reducing labour en masse. This also seems to be the view of joint CD Projekt Red CEO Michał Nowakowski, who was asked such a question during an earnings conference yesterday, and once more found himself required to emphasise that they're using people to make videogames like The Witcher 4: "AI is definitely becoming a thing in games development as well. We are still predominantly using people and this is our plan—to make games where we're not walking away from that." title: Corsair HS35 v3 review
summary: A very affordable mid-range headset that pulls off everything with aplomb, offering no surprises whether good or bad.
body: If you skipped buying that coveted stick of RAM or 2 TB SSD this time last year, you must be feeling understandably morose. Most things are getting more and more expensive, but crucially, not all things. Components like headsets and gamepads conform to the fast antiquating dictum that, with time, value will rise while costs decrease. That's pretty much the case with the Corsair HS35 v3. At the level of raw specs at least, Corsair's new mid-range headset has a touch more to offer than the SteelSeries Arctic Nova 3X, which is our favourite mid-range gaming headset. It came bearing a $90 price tag at launch (though you wouldn't pay full price for it in 2026). Like the Arctis Nova 3X, the HS35 v3 has 2.4 GHz wireless connectivity, Bluetooth, and a wired option. It has a detachable mic, and reasonably comfortable memory foam ear cups. Both models have 50mm drivers and a 20Hz - 20kHz frequency response. But the HS35 v3 is 10 grams lighter and $10 cheaper. Shots fired!
